## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Geometric Data Analysis
  Official title       Geometric data analysis
  Instructors          J. FEYDY (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 21 h (lectures 14 h, labs 7 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label}[Track Santé]{.badge .track}
  Language             not displayed on master-mva.com or on the Université Paris-Saclay course detail (the master-mva.com description is written in English)
  Assessment           master-mva.com: “Project report and presentation (15 points) + quizz (5 points)”; joint projects with other classes are welcome; in-person attendance is preferable, but the class may be validated remotely; video recordings of the lectures are available. Université Paris-Saclay course detail: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment).
  Prerequisites        Linear algebra, basic programming with Python (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with an M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who has trained a few models and wants to know which representation, distance and loss to use for vectors, graphs, surfaces and probability distributions.

**Empirical first**: in dimension 1000, the farthest of 1000 uniform points is only 11 % farther from a query than the nearest one (Code 1.4). Moreover, a gradient flow driven by a Gaussian kernel norm with a narrow kernel leaves every point stranded, while the same flow driven by optimal transport brings all of them to the target (Code 6.16). Both facts are geometric, and this course explains them.

The course gives one geometric viewpoint on common machine learning models. Data are vectors, points on a curved space, nodes of a graph or samples of a distribution; each choice comes with its own distances, convolutions and losses, and with its own computational cost. The course is a hub for the Santé track and for the geometry-oriented courses: [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html), [Geometry Processing and Geometric Deep Learning](../s1-geometry-processing-gdl/index.html), [Geometry and Shape Spaces](../s2-shape-spaces/index.html) and [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Explain the curse of dimensionality with exact computations, and say when a nearest-neighbour or kernel method can still work.
-   Encode an invariance in a distance, and compute shape distances on Kendall's sphere of triangles.
-   Compare decision trees, nearest neighbours, linear models, neural networks and kernel methods by the geometry they impose on the feature space.
-   Choose between a squared loss and a cross-entropy, and justify the choice by gradients and by the geometry of the simplex.
-   Estimate the intrinsic dimension of a data set, measure curvature, and build graph-based embeddings (Isomap, Laplacian eigenmaps, t-SNE, UMAP).
-   Write a graph convolution and a rotation-equivariant layer from scratch, and prove their equivariance.
-   Compute distances, geodesics and Fréchet means on the sphere and in the Poincaré disk, and measure the error of graph shortest paths.
-   Compare probability distributions with divergences, the Fisher–Rao metric, kernel norms and optimal transport, and implement the Sinkhorn algorithm.
-   Relate kernel matrices, graphs, heat kernels, entropic transport plans and attention matrices to one another.
-   Predict whether a computation is memory-bound or compute-bound, and write a tiled reduction that never stores an $M \times N$ matrix.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com sums up the objective as “choosing the correct loss, distance and convolution for every problem”. It presents machine learning as the meeting point of modelling, software engineering and statistics. In that setting, geometry encodes expert knowledge: well-chosen distances between samples enforce fundamental properties while keeping a simple mathematical form.

The description stresses structured data, such as anatomical images, protein conformations and physical simulations. Its purpose is a unifying geometric perspective on common models, so that students can answer three questions. Should data be represented by vectors, graphs or histograms? How much does the choice between a Euclidean norm and a cross-entropy matter? How are kernels, graphs, manifolds, optimal transport and transformer networks related?

master-mva.com organises the course in seven lectures of three hours, five of which include a lab session. The “Thèmes abordés” section presents the class as foundational background for geometry in machine learning and lists the courses of both semesters for which it is useful. ### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: linear algebra and basic programming with Python (master-mva.com). The instructor listed on master-mva.com is Jean Feydy. The course carries the label of the Santé track and is taught in period 1, so only the refreshers come before it.

-   **Refreshers** — [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) for the spectral theorem and gradients; [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) for Gaussian vectors and divergences; [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) for the labs.
-   **Related courses of semester 1** — [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html), [Geometry Processing and Geometric Deep Learning](../s1-geometry-processing-gdl/index.html), [Topological Data Analysis](../s1-tda-imaging-ml/index.html), [Medical Image Analysis](../s1-medical-image-analysis/index.html), [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) and [3D Computer Vision](../s1-3d-computer-vision/index.html).
-   **Courses of semester 2 that build on it** — [Geometry and Shape Spaces](../s2-shape-spaces/index.html), [Kernel Methods](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html), [Point Clouds and 3D Modelling](../s2-point-clouds-3d/index.html), [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html), [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html), [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html), [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html), [Deformable Models and Geodesic Methods](../s2-deformable-models-geodesics/index.html) and [Algorithms and Learning for Protein Science](../s2-protein-science/index.html).
-   **Computation** — [Training and Deploying Large-Scale Models](../s2-training-deploying-large-models/index.html) continues ch. 7 at the scale of large networks.
-   **Afterwards** — the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html); the [Hospital Immersion](../year-hospital-immersion/index.html) of the Santé track gives a clinical context to the medical case studies.

### Course outline

-   **Review: linear algebra, probability and numerics** — inner products and the Gram trick, the spectral theorem, Gaussian vectors, softmax, cross-entropy and the stable log-sum-exp.
-   **Why geometry?** — the curse of dimensionality, invariant distances, Kendall's sphere of triangles, style transfer as a comparison of feature distributions.
-   **Flat vector spaces** — trees, nearest neighbours, linear models, neural networks and kernels, read as choices of geometry on $\mathbb{R}^d$.
-   **Graphs and embeddings** — Gaussian bubbles, the manifold hypothesis, intrinsic dimension, curvature, neighbourhood graphs and embeddings.
-   **Geometric deep learning** — graph convolutions, equivariant layers, five challenges, protein docking and lung registration, learned graphs and attention.
-   **Riemannian metrics and geodesics** — metrics, the Poincaré disk, discrete and continuous shortest paths, Fréchet means.
-   **Probability distributions** — divergences, information geometry, kernel norms, optimal transport and the Sinkhorn algorithm; one matrix read five ways.
-   **GPU programming** — the hardware, the roofline model, tiled reductions with an online log-sum-exp, and the end of Dennard scaling.
-   **Complements for self-study** — the proofs left out of the sessions, Ollivier–Ricci curvature, trees in the hyperbolic plane, convergence and debiasing of Sinkhorn, the graph Laplacian as a Laplace–Beltrami operator.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — scalable geometric computing, equivariance, protein design, unbalanced transport, transformers as interacting particles (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read [ch. 0](#ch0) before session 1, even if it looks familiar: the Gram trick (Proposition 0.2) and the stable log-sum-exp (Proposition 0.9) come back in ch. 3, 4, 6 and 7.
-   Follow one thread through the page: a Gaussian kernel matrix is a similarity (ch. 2), a weighted graph (ch. 3), a heat kernel (ch. 5), an entropic transport plan and an attention matrix (ch. 6), and a reduction to compute fast (ch. 7).
-   After each session, run the code of the chapter and change one parameter (dimension, kernel width, $\varepsilon$, tile size) to see what breaks.
-   Do the exercises listed in the session plan before the next session, and read the proofs of [ch. 8](#ch8) after the session that states the result. The ★★★ exercises and the projects prepare the project report, which carries 15 of the 20 points.
-   Python environment: NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, NetworkX and PyTorch on CPU; every code block runs in under 30 seconds. The official labs use UMAP, PyTorch Geometric, GeomStats and GeomLoss; the code here rewrites the needed parts in plain NumPy and PyTorch so that nothing else must be installed.

## 0. Review: linear algebra, probability and numerics {#ch0}

Every chapter compares data points, and every comparison is computed from inner products, eigenvalues or logarithms of sums of exponentials. This chapter states these M1 tools in the form used later, with short proofs.

### 0.1 Inner products and the Gram trick

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Inner product, norm, distance]{.tag} An inner product on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a symmetric bilinear form with $\langle x, x \rangle > 0$ for $x \neq 0$. It defines the norm $\|x\| = \sqrt{\langle x, x \rangle}$ and the distance $d(x, y) = \|x - y\|$.

Every inner product reads $\langle x, y \rangle_M = x^\top M y$ for a symmetric positive definite matrix $M$. Choosing $M$ means choosing which directions of the data matter.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — The Gram trick]{.tag} For $x_1, \dots, x_M$ and $y_1, \dots, y_N$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the matrix of squared distances is
$$
\big( \|x_i - y_j\|^2 \big)_{ij} = \big( \|x_i\|^2 \big)_i \mathbf{1}^\top + \mathbf{1} \big( \|y_j\|^2 \big)_j^\top - 2\, X Y^\top ,
$$
where $X$ and $Y$ stack the points as rows.

::: proof
Expand $\|x - y\|^2 = \langle x - y, x - y \rangle$ by bilinearity and symmetry. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

All pairwise distances therefore cost one matrix product, the fastest operation on modern hardware (ch. 7).

### 0.2 Spectral theorem and positive matrices

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.3 — Spectral theorem and singular value decomposition]{.tag} A real symmetric matrix $S$ factors as $S = U \Lambda U^\top$ with $U$ orthogonal and $\Lambda$ real diagonal.

Any real matrix factors as $A = U \Sigma V^\top$ with $U, V$ orthogonal and $\Sigma \geq 0$ diagonal.

::: proof
See the [linear algebra refresher](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html); the second statement follows from the first applied to $A^\top A$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — Positive semi-definite matrix]{.tag} A symmetric matrix $K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is positive semi-definite (PSD) if $c^\top K c \geq 0$ for all $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$, that is, if its eigenvalues are non-negative.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — PSD matrices are Gram matrices]{.tag} $K$ is PSD if and only if there are vectors $z_1, \dots, z_n$ with
$$
K_{ij} = \langle z_i, z_j \rangle .
$$

::: proof
If $K_{ij} = \langle z_i, z_j \rangle$, then $c^\top K c = \| \sum_i c_i z_i \|^2 \geq 0$.

Conversely, write $K = U \Lambda U^\top$ with $\Lambda \geq 0$, and take for $z_i$ the $i$-th row of $U \Lambda^{1/2}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A PSD similarity matrix is therefore an inner product between hidden feature vectors (ch. 2 and 3).

### 0.3 Gaussian vectors

::: def
[Definition 0.6 — Standard Gaussian vector]{.tag} $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ has independent $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ coordinates and density
$$
p(x) = (2\pi)^{-d/2} \exp\big( -\|x\|^2 / 2 \big) .
$$
Its law is invariant under every orthogonal transformation.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.7 — Moments of the squared norm]{.tag} If $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$, then
$$
\mathbb{E} \|X\|^2 = d, \qquad \operatorname{Var} \|X\|^2 = 2d .
$$

::: proof
$\|X\|^2 = \sum_k X_k^2$ is a sum of $d$ independent terms with $\mathbb{E} X_k^2 = 1$ and $\mathbb{E} X_k^4 = 3$, so each term has variance $3 - 1 = 2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 0.4 Softmax, cross-entropy and the log-sum-exp

::: def
[Definition 0.8 — Softmax, cross-entropy, Kullback–Leibler divergence]{.tag} For scores $s \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and distributions $p, q$ on $\{1, \dots, n\}$:
$$
\operatorname{softmax}(s)_i = \frac{e^{s_i}}{\sum_j e^{s_j}}, \qquad H(q, p) = -\sum_i q_i \log p_i, \qquad \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \sum_i q_i \log \frac{q_i}{p_i} .
$$
The cross-entropy decomposes as $H(q, p) = H(q) + \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)$, where $H(q) = H(q, q)$ is the entropy.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.9 — Gibbs inequality and stable log-sum-exp]{.tag} (a) $\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) \geq 0$, with equality if and only if $p = q$.

(b) For every $s \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $m = \max_j s_j$,
$$
\log \sum_j e^{s_j} = m + \log \sum_j e^{s_j - m} ,
$$
and every exponential on the right lies in $(0, 1]$.

::: proof
(a) By Jensen's inequality for the concave logarithm,
$$
-\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \sum_i q_i \log \frac{p_i}{q_i} \leq \log \sum_i p_i = 0 ,
$$
with equality only if $p_i / q_i$ is constant on the support of $q$.

(b) Factor $e^{m}$ out of the sum. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Code 0.10 — Distances by the Gram trick and a stable log-sum-exp]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X, Y = rng.normal(size=(5, 3)), rng.normal(size=(4, 3))
# |x - y|^2 = |x|^2 + |y|^2 - 2 <x, y>: all distances from one matrix product (Proposition 0.2)
D2 = (X**2).sum(1)[:, None] + (Y**2).sum(1)[None, :] - 2 * X @ Y.T
print("Gram trick error:", np.abs(D2 - ((X[:, None] - Y[None]) ** 2).sum(-1)).max())

def logsumexp(s):
    """log sum_j exp(s_j), computed without overflow (Proposition 0.9)."""
    m = s.max()
    return m + np.log(np.exp(s - m).sum())

s = np.array([1000.0, 999.0, 990.0])
with np.errstate(over="ignore"):
    print("naive:", np.log(np.exp(s).sum()), "  stable:", round(logsumexp(s), 6))
p = np.exp(s - logsumexp(s))                       # softmax
q = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.2])
print("softmax:", np.round(p, 4), "  KL(q || p) =", round(float(np.sum(q * np.log(q / p))), 4))
```

The Gram trick agrees with the direct computation to $10^{-15}$; the naive log-sum-exp overflows, the stable one returns 1000.3133. The softmax gives the third score a mass $4.5 \times 10^{-5}$ where $q$ puts 20 %, hence $\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = 1.58$.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   An inner product is a choice of geometry; pairwise distances cost one matrix product.
-   PSD matrices are Gram matrices; $\|X\|^2 = d \pm \sqrt{2d}$ for a standard Gaussian.
-   Softmax, cross-entropy and KL go through the log-sum-exp, shifted by its maximum.
:::

## 1. Why geometry? {#ch1}

Distances between raw vectors stop being informative in high dimension, yet real data are learnable. This chapter measures the problem, then shows how a well-chosen geometry, one that encodes the invariances of the data, solves it.

### 1.1 The curse of dimensionality

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.1 — Volume lives near the boundary]{.tag} In $\mathbb{R}^d$, the fraction of the volume of the unit ball lying within $\varepsilon$ of its boundary is
$$
1 - (1 - \varepsilon)^d \geq 1 - e^{-\varepsilon d} .
$$

::: proof
The volume of the ball of radius $r$ is $c_d\, r^d$, so the inner ball of radius $1 - \varepsilon$ holds a fraction $(1 - \varepsilon)^d \leq e^{-\varepsilon d}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For $d = 100$ and $\varepsilon = 0.05$, the shell holds 99.4 % of the volume.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Covering numbers]{.tag} Covering the cube $[0, 1]^d$ with cubes of side $2\varepsilon$ requires at least
$$
N(\varepsilon) \geq (2 \varepsilon)^{-d}
$$
cubes.

::: proof
Each small cube has volume $(2\varepsilon)^d$, and their union must have volume at least 1. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Local methods ($k$-NN, kernels of width $\varepsilon$) average labels over such cells: with $\varepsilon = 0.1$ in dimension 10, there are $5^{10} \approx 10^7$ cells to fill.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — Concentration of distances]{.tag} Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent and uniform on $[0, 1]^d$. Then
$$
\mathbb{E} \|X - Y\|^2 = \frac{d}{6}, \qquad \frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var} \|X - Y\|^2}}{\mathbb{E} \|X - Y\|^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1.4}{d}} .
$$

::: proof
For one coordinate, $T = U - V$ has the triangular density $1 - |t|$ on $[-1, 1]$. Hence
$$
\mathbb{E} T^2 = 2 \int_0^1 t^2 (1 - t)\, dt = \frac16, \qquad \mathbb{E} T^4 = 2 \int_0^1 t^4 (1 - t)\, dt = \frac{1}{15} .
$$

So $\operatorname{Var} T^2 = 1/15 - 1/36 = 7/180$. The $d$ coordinates are independent, so the mean and variance are multiplied by $d$, and the ratio is $\sqrt{7d/180} \cdot 6/d = \sqrt{1.4/d}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

By Chebyshev's inequality, all distances from a query are then within a few percent of each other.

::: ex
[Code 1.4 — Relative contrast of distances]{.tag} For 1000 uniform points and a uniform query, the code prints $(\max - \min) / \min$ of the distances to the query.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 1000                                   # points per data set
for d in [2, 10, 100, 1000]:
    X, q = rng.random((n, d)), rng.random(d)   # uniform cloud and a query
    dist = np.linalg.norm(X - q, axis=1)
    contrast = (dist.max() - dist.min()) / dist.min()
    print(f"d = {d:4d}:  relative contrast = {contrast:6.2f},  "
          f"mean squared distance / d = {np.mean(dist**2) / d:.3f}")
```

The contrast falls from 134.6 ($d = 2$) to 3.48, 0.39 and 0.11 ($d = 1000$), and the mean squared distance over $d$ tends to $1/6$.
:::

Real data escape this curse: they concentrate near low-dimensional sets (ch. 3), and their labels are invariant under known transformations, which a distance can quotient out.

### 1.2 Geometry as a modelling tool

::: def
[Definition 1.5 — Invariant distance and quotient distance]{.tag} Let a group $G$ act on a metric space $(\mathcal{X}, d)$. The distance is $G$-invariant if $d(g \cdot x, g \cdot y) = d(x, y)$ for all $g, x, y$. The quotient distance between orbits is
$$
\bar d([x], [y]) = \inf_{g \in G} d(x, g \cdot y) .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.6 — The quotient distance is a pseudo-distance]{.tag} If $d$ is $G$-invariant, then $\bar d$ does not depend on the chosen representatives, and it is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality.

::: proof
*Representatives*: by invariance,
$$
d(h \cdot x, g k \cdot y) = d(x, h^{-1} g k \cdot y) ,
$$
and $h^{-1} g k$ runs over $G$ when $g$ does.

*Symmetry*: $d(x, g \cdot y) = d(g^{-1} \cdot x, y)$.

*Triangle inequality*: for all $g, h$,
$$
d(x, g \cdot z) \leq d(x, h \cdot y) + d(y, h^{-1} g \cdot z) .
$$
Take the infimum over $g$, then over $h$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Translations of images (registration), rotations of molecules (alignment before a root-mean-square deviation), relabellings of the points of a cloud (ch. 6) and reparametrizations of curves are all quotiented this way.

### 1.3 The sphere of triangles

A triangle is a vector $z = (z_1, z_2, z_3) \in \mathbb{C}^3$ of vertices, and its shape is what remains after translations, rotations and scalings $z \mapsto a z + b$, with $a \in \mathbb{C}^*$ and $b \in \mathbb{C}$. The Helmert coordinates
$$
u = \frac{z_2 - z_1}{\sqrt 2}, \qquad v = \frac{2 z_3 - z_1 - z_2}{\sqrt 6}
$$
remove translations isometrically. Scaling is removed by imposing $|u|^2 + |v|^2 = 1$, and rotations act as $(u, v) \mapsto e^{i\theta} (u, v)$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.7 — Kendall's sphere of triangles]{.tag} The map
$$
h(u, v) = \big( |u|^2 - |v|^2,\ 2 \operatorname{Re}(u \bar v),\ 2 \operatorname{Im}(u \bar v) \big)
$$
identifies the shapes of triangles with the unit sphere $S^2$. The Procrustes distance $\rho = \arccos |\langle (u, v), (u', v') \rangle|$ between two shapes satisfies
$$
\angle\big( h(u, v), h(u', v') \big) = 2 \rho ,
$$
so the shape space is a sphere of radius $1/2$. Equilateral triangles of either orientation map to the two poles, and collinear triangles to the equator.

::: proof
1.  *Invariance and image*: $h$ is unchanged by a common phase $e^{i\theta}$, and
    $$
    \|h\|^2 = (|u|^2 - |v|^2)^2 + 4 |u|^2 |v|^2 = (|u|^2 + |v|^2)^2 = 1 .
    $$
2.  *Fibres*: $h$ gives $|u|^2$, $|v|^2$ and $u \bar v$, which determine $(u, v)$ up to a common phase. Every point of $S^2$ is reached.
3.  *Distances*: a direct expansion gives, for unit vectors $a, b \in \mathbb{C}^2$,
    $$
    h(a) \cdot h(b) = 2\, |\langle a, b \rangle|^2 - 1 = \cos(2\rho) .
    $$
4.  *Poles and equator*: the third coordinate equals $-4\sqrt3\, A / (a^2 + b^2 + c^2)$, with $A$ the signed area and $a, b, c$ the side lengths. It is $\pm 1$ exactly for equilateral triangles (Weitzenböck's inequality) and 0 for collinear ones. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

If the three vertices are independent standard complex Gaussians, $(u, v)$ is a standard Gaussian vector of $\mathbb{C}^2$. Its normalization is uniform on $S^3$, and the map $h$ pushes it to the uniform law on $S^2$. By Archimedes' theorem, the third coordinate is then uniform on $[-1, 1]$.

::: ex
[Code 1.8 — Triangles on the sphere]{.tag} The code maps triangles to $S^2$, checks the factor 2 of Theorem 1.7, and samples Gaussian triangles.

```python
import numpy as np

def shape_point(z):
    """Point of the unit sphere S^2 representing the triangles z (rows of 3 complex vertices)."""
    u = (z[:, 1] - z[:, 0]) / np.sqrt(2)              # Helmert coordinates: translations removed
    v = (2 * z[:, 2] - z[:, 0] - z[:, 1]) / np.sqrt(6)
    r2 = abs(u)**2 + abs(v)**2                          # scale removed by dividing by r2
    w = u * np.conj(v)                                  # rotations z -> e^{it} z leave w unchanged
    return np.c_[(abs(u)**2 - abs(v)**2), 2 * w.real, 2 * w.imag] / r2[:, None]

def kendall(z1, z2):
    """Procrustes distance rho = arccos |<z1, z2>| between centred, normalized triangles."""
    a = np.c_[(z1[1] - z1[0]) / np.sqrt(2), (2 * z1[2] - z1[0] - z1[1]) / np.sqrt(6)].ravel()
    b = np.c_[(z2[1] - z2[0]) / np.sqrt(2), (2 * z2[2] - z2[0] - z2[1]) / np.sqrt(6)].ravel()
    c = abs(np.vdot(a, b)) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
    return np.arccos(min(c, 1.0))

equi = np.array([0, 1, np.exp(1j * np.pi / 3)])
flat = np.array([0, 1, 3 + 0j])
right = np.array([0, 1, 1j])
moved = 2.5 * np.exp(0.8j) * right + (4 - 1j)            # a similar copy of `right`
P = shape_point(np.vstack([equi, np.conj(equi), flat, right, moved]))
print("sphere points (equilateral, mirror, collinear, right, moved right):")
print(np.round(P, 4))
ang = np.arccos(np.clip(P[0] @ P[3], -1, 1))
print(f"angle on S^2 = {ang:.4f},  2 * Kendall distance = {2 * kendall(equi, right):.4f}")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)                            # Gaussian random triangles
n = 200_000
Z = rng.normal(size=(n, 3)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(n, 3))
h3 = shape_point(Z)[:, 2]
print("quartiles of the third coordinate:", np.round(np.quantile(h3, [0.25, 0.5, 0.75]), 3))
s = np.sort(np.c_[abs(Z[:, 0] - Z[:, 1]), abs(Z[:, 1] - Z[:, 2]), abs(Z[:, 2] - Z[:, 0])]**2, axis=1)
print(f"fraction of obtuse triangles = {np.mean(s[:, 2] > s[:, 0] + s[:, 1]):.4f}")
```

The equilateral triangle and its mirror land on the poles, the collinear triangle on the equator, and the right triangle and its moved copy on the same point. The angle 0.5236 is twice the Kendall distance $\pi / 12$.

The quartiles of the third coordinate are close to $-0.5, 0, 0.5$, and 74.96 % of Gaussian triangles are obtuse, close to the exact value $3/4$.
:::

### 1.4 Deep Art

Style transfer (Gatys, Ecker and Bethge, 2016) optimizes an image $x$ so that its deep features resemble those of a content image $c$ at one layer, and those of a style image $s$ at several layers, through Gram matrices.

::: def
[Definition 1.9 — Gram matrix of features and style loss]{.tag} Let $F^l(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{C_l \times N_l}$ hold the $C_l$ channels of layer $l$ of a fixed network at $N_l$ positions, with columns $f_1, \dots, f_{N_l}$. Its Gram matrix and the transfer loss are
$$
G^l(x) = \frac{1}{N_l} F^l(x) F^l(x)^\top, \qquad \mathcal{L}(x) = \|F^L(x) - F^L(c)\|^2 + \lambda \sum_l w_l\, \|G^l(x) - G^l(s)\|_F^2 .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.10 — Style is a distribution of features]{.tag} (a) $G^l$ is invariant under every permutation of the $N_l$ positions.

(b) Let $\mu_a = \frac1N \sum_i \delta_{f_i}$ and $\mu_b = \frac1M \sum_j \delta_{g_j}$ be the empirical feature distributions of two images. With $k(f, g) = \langle f, g \rangle^2$,
$$
\|G_a - G_b\|_F^2 = \iint k(f, g)\, d(\mu_a - \mu_b)(f)\, d(\mu_a - \mu_b)(g) .
$$

::: proof
(a) $F F^\top = \sum_i f_i f_i^\top$ does not depend on the order of the columns.

(b) The Frobenius inner product of two Gram matrices is
$$
\langle G_a, G_b \rangle_F = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{i, j} \operatorname{tr}\big( f_i f_i^\top g_j g_j^\top \big) = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{i, j} \langle f_i, g_j \rangle^2 .
$$
Expand $\|G_a - G_b\|_F^2$ into three such terms. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Content is compared as a vector and style as a histogram of features. The right-hand side of (b) is a kernel norm between distributions (ch. 6); Kolkin, Salavon and Shakhnarovich (2019) replaced it by optimal transport.

::: ex
[Code 1.11 — Pixel distance versus style distance]{.tag} A striped texture is compared with a shifted copy, a copy with shuffled $16 \times 16$ tiles, and stripes of another orientation. Features come from 16 random filters and a ReLU, so nothing is downloaded.

```python
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)
torch.set_num_threads(1)
n = 64
y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(n), torch.arange(n), indexing="ij")

def texture(theta):
    """Stripes of orientation theta plus a little noise: a 1 x 1 x n x n image."""
    img = torch.sin(0.6 * (x * torch.cos(theta) + y * torch.sin(theta))) + 0.3 * torch.randn(n, n)
    return img[None, None].float()

conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(1, 16, 5, padding=2, padding_mode="circular", bias=False)

def features(img):                       # 16 random filters + ReLU, flattened: 16 x n^2
    with torch.no_grad():
        return torch.relu(conv(img))[0].reshape(16, -1)

def gram(F):                             # second moments of the feature distribution
    return F @ F.T / F.shape[1]

a = texture(torch.tensor(0.4))
b = torch.roll(a, shifts=(17, 29), dims=(2, 3))                       # same texture, shifted
tiles = a.reshape(1, 1, 4, 16, 4, 16).permute(0, 1, 2, 4, 3, 5).reshape(1, 1, 16, 16, 16)
c = tiles[:, :, torch.randperm(16)].reshape(1, 1, 4, 4, 16, 16).permute(0, 1, 2, 4, 3, 5).reshape(1, 1, n, n)
d = texture(torch.tensor(1.6))                                        # other orientation

Ga = gram(features(a))
for name, img in [("shifted", b), ("tiles shuffled", c), ("other texture", d)]:
    pix = (img - a).norm() / a.norm()
    sty = (gram(features(img)) - Ga).norm() / Ga.norm()
    print(f"{name:15s}: pixel distance {pix:.3f}   Gram (style) distance {sty:.3f}")
```

In pixels, the three images are equally far from the original (1.44, 1.43, 1.41). The style distance separates them: 0.000 for the shift, 0.098 for the shuffled tiles (tile borders change a few features), 0.606 for the other orientation.
:::

### 1.5 Overview of the class

::: note
[Overview 1.12 — Data, representations and geometries]{.tag}

| Data | Representation | Geometry | Chapter |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tabular features, images as arrays | vectors of $\mathbb{R}^d$ | norms, inner products, kernels | ch. 2 |
| Point clouds, meshes, molecules, social networks | graphs, manifolds | graph Laplacians, geodesics, curvature, equivariance | ch. 3–5 |
| Histograms, densities, populations, shapes as measures | probability distributions | divergences, Fisher–Rao, kernel norms, optimal transport | ch. 6 |
| All of the above, at scale | arrays on a GPU | arithmetic intensity, memory traffic | ch. 7 |
:::

The three questions of the official objective run through this table: vectors, graphs or histograms is a choice of row; the norm against the cross-entropy is a geometry on the simplex (ch. 2, 6); kernels, graphs, manifolds, transport and transformers meet in one matrix (Section 6.5).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   In high dimension, volume sits near the boundary, covering needs $\varepsilon^{-d}$ cells, and distances concentrate.
-   Quotienting an invariant distance by a group turns invariances into geometry.
-   Triangle shapes form a sphere of radius $1/2$, on which Gaussian triangles are uniform.
-   Style transfer compares feature distributions through Gram matrices, a kernel norm.
:::

## 2. Flat vector spaces {#ch2}

The classical model families all work in $\mathbb{R}^d$, but each one imposes its own geometry. This chapter asks two questions of each model: which transformations of the features leave it unchanged, and how it decides that two points are close.

### 2.1 Decision trees

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Decision tree, CART]{.tag} A decision tree partitions $\mathbb{R}^d$ into axis-aligned boxes by recursive tests $x_k \leq t$, and predicts the majority label (or the mean) of each leaf. CART chooses each split greedily, to minimize the weighted impurity of the two children, for instance the Gini impurity
$$
G(p) = 1 - \sum_c p_c^2 .
$$
:::

For a node with 5 samples of each class, $G = 0.5$. A split into children $(4, 1)$ and $(1, 4)$ gives $G = 1 - 0.64 - 0.04 = 0.32$ in each child, a gain of $0.18$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Trees ignore monotone changes of units]{.tag} If each feature is transformed by a strictly increasing map $\varphi_k$, CART builds the same partition of the training samples, with transformed thresholds. Rotations of the feature space, in contrast, change the tree.

::: proof
The test $x_k \leq t$ selects the same samples as $\varphi_k(x_k) \leq \varphi_k(t)$. Impurities depend only on the induced partition of the samples, so the same splits are available with the same costs at every node.

For rotations, a boundary $x_1 = x_2$ is a single oblique line, but an axis-aligned tree can only approximate it by a staircase of many splits. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 2.2 Nearest neighbours

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — $k$-nearest-neighbour rule]{.tag} Given training pairs $(x_i, y_i)$ and a distance $d$, the $k$-NN rule predicts at a new point the majority label among the $k$ training points closest to it for $d$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.4 — Cover and Hart, 1967]{.tag} For binary classification with $\eta(x) = \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid X = x)$ continuous, the risk of the 1-NN rule tends, as $n \to \infty$, to
$$
R_1 = \mathbb{E}\big[ 2 \eta(X) (1 - \eta(X)) \big] \leq 2 R^\star (1 - R^\star),
$$
where $R^\star = \mathbb{E} \min(\eta(X), 1 - \eta(X))$ is the Bayes risk.

A proof sketch is in [ch. 8](#ch8).
::::

At finite $n$, however, the distance decides which points are neighbours, and the sample size needed grows like $\varepsilon^{-d}$ (Proposition 1.2). The rule is invariant under isometries of $d$, not under changes of units.

### 2.3 Linear models and losses

::: def
[Definition 2.5 — Linear and logistic models]{.tag} A linear model scores $f(x) = \langle w, x \rangle + b$. Logistic regression predicts
$$
\mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(f(x)), \qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} ,
$$
and its multiclass version predicts $\operatorname{softmax}(W x + b)$.
:::

An invertible affine change of features, $x \mapsto A x + c$, maps the set of linear models onto itself through $w \mapsto A^{-\top} w$. Only the regularization $\|w\|^2$ sees the geometry of the features.

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Squared loss and cross-entropy]{.tag} For a predicted distribution $p$ on the classes and a label $y$, with $e_y$ the one-hot vector:
$$
\ell_2(p, y) = \|p - e_y\|^2, \qquad \ell_{\mathrm{CE}}(p, y) = -\log p_y = \mathrm{KL}(e_y \,\|\, p) .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.7 — Gradients of the two losses]{.tag} For a binary label $y \in \{0, 1\}$ and $p = \sigma(z)$,
$$
\frac{\partial \ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial z} = p - y, \qquad \frac{\partial (p - y)^2}{\partial z} = 2 (p - y)\, p (1 - p) .
$$
The cross-entropy is convex in $z$; the squared loss is not, and its gradient vanishes when $p$ saturates at the wrong value.

::: proof
Use $\sigma' = \sigma (1 - \sigma)$. For $y = 1$, the derivative of $-\log \sigma(z)$ is $-(1 - \sigma) = p - 1$.

For $y = 0$, the derivative of $-\log(1 - \sigma(z))$ is $\sigma = p$.

The second derivative of the cross-entropy is $p (1 - p) > 0$. The squared loss gradient carries the factor $p(1 - p)$, which tends to 0 when $z \to \pm \infty$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.8 — A confident mistake]{.tag} Take $z = -5$ and $y = 1$, so $p = \sigma(-5) = 0.0067$. The cross-entropy gradient is $-0.9933$. The squared-loss gradient is
$$
2 \times (-0.9933) \times 0.0067 \times 0.9933 = -0.0132 ,
$$
75 times smaller: the squared loss barely corrects a confident mistake.
:::

Geometrically, $\ell_2$ measures the simplex with the Euclidean metric, while $\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}$ is a Kullback–Leibler divergence, which blows up near the faces of the simplex: confident errors cost a lot. For regression with Gaussian noise, the squared loss is the right choice, being the negative log-likelihood.

### 2.4 Neural networks

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.9 — ReLU networks are piecewise affine]{.tag} A network that alternates affine maps and $\operatorname{ReLU}(t) = \max(0, t)$ is continuous, and $\mathbb{R}^d$ splits into finitely many polyhedra on each of which it is affine.

::: proof
By induction on the layers. An affine map of a piecewise affine function is piecewise affine. Applying the ReLU coordinatewise refines each polyhedron by the hyperplane where the pre-activation changes sign. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A ReLU network thus learns its own partition, like a tree with oblique cells; universal approximation (Cybenko, 1989) is the limit of this picture. On raw vectors it treats coordinates as unrelated, and structure enters through weight sharing.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.10 — Translation-equivariant linear maps are convolutions]{.tag} Let $L : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ act on signals indexed by $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ and commute with every translation $(\tau_s x)_i = x_{i - s}$. With $h = L e_0$,
$$
(L x)_i = \sum_j h_{i - j}\, x_j .
$$

::: proof
Write $x = \sum_j x_j e_j = \sum_j x_j \tau_j e_0$. By linearity and equivariance,
$$
L x = \sum_j x_j\, \tau_j L e_0 = \sum_j x_j\, \tau_j h .
$$
Read the $i$-th coordinate. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Convolutions are therefore exactly the linear layers that respect translations. Replacing translations by permutations of graph nodes or by rotations of space gives the layers of ch. 4.

### 2.5 Kernel methods

::: def
[Definition 2.11 — Positive definite kernel and RKHS]{.tag} A function $k : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a positive definite kernel if every matrix $(k(x_i, x_j))_{ij}$ is PSD. Its reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_k$ is the completion of the span of the functions $k(\cdot, x)$ for the inner product
$$
\langle k(\cdot, x), k(\cdot, y) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}} = k(x, y) ,
$$
so that $f(x) = \langle f, k(\cdot, x) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}}$. The Gaussian kernel is $k(x, y) = \exp(-\|x - y\|^2 / 2\sigma^2)$.
:::

By Proposition 0.5, a kernel is an inner product between feature vectors $\varphi(x) = k(\cdot, x)$. A kernel method is a linear method in the geometry of that feature space, where
$$
\|\varphi(x) - \varphi(y)\|^2 = k(x, x) + k(y, y) - 2 k(x, y) .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.12 — Representer theorem]{.tag} For any loss $L$ and $\lambda > 0$, a minimizer over $\mathcal{H}_k$ of
$$
\sum_{i = 1}^n L\big( y_i, f(x_i) \big) + \lambda \|f\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2
$$
can be sought as $f = \sum_i \alpha_i k(\cdot, x_i)$. For the squared loss, $\alpha = (K + \lambda I)^{-1} y$ with $K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)$.

::: proof
Split $f = f_\parallel + f_\perp$, with $f_\parallel$ in the span of the $k(\cdot, x_i)$. Then $f_\perp(x_i) = \langle f_\perp, k(\cdot, x_i) \rangle = 0$, so the data term only depends on $f_\parallel$, while
$$
\|f\|^2 = \|f_\parallel\|^2 + \|f_\perp\|^2 .
$$
A minimizer therefore has $f_\perp = 0$.

For the squared loss, the objective $\|y - K \alpha\|^2 + \lambda\, \alpha^\top K \alpha$ has gradient $2 K \big( (K + \lambda I) \alpha - y \big)$, which vanishes at the stated $\alpha$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The width $\sigma$ sets the geometry. When $\sigma \to 0$, the Gaussian kernel only sees the nearest points, as $k$-NN does; when $\sigma$ is large, it behaves like a low-degree polynomial. A kernel matrix is also a weighted neighbourhood graph, the starting point of ch. 3.

::: ex
[Code 2.13 — Lab: the scikit-learn classifiers]{.tag} Five classifiers are trained on two noisy half-moons, then on the same data with the second feature multiplied by 100 (a change of units), and on the data rotated by $45°$.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC

X, y = make_moons(n_samples=600, noise=0.25, random_state=0)
R = np.array([[1, 1], [-1, 1]]) / np.sqrt(2)                 # rotation by 45 degrees
versions = {"original": X,
            "x2 scaled by 100": X * [1, 100],              # change of units on one feature
            "rotated by 45 deg": X @ R.T}
models = {"tree (depth 6)": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=6, random_state=0),
          "15-NN": KNeighborsClassifier(15),
          "logistic": LogisticRegression(),
          "MLP 32-32": MLPClassifier((32, 32), max_iter=2000, random_state=0),
          "SVM, Gaussian": SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma=2.0)}
print(f"{'':16s}" + "".join(f"{k:>20s}" for k in versions))
for name, model in models.items():
    accs = []
    for Xv in versions.values():
        Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xv, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=0)
        accs.append(model.fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte))
    print(f"{name:16s}" + "".join(f"{a:20.3f}" for a in accs))
```

On the original data, the four non-linear models reach 0.90 to 0.91 and the linear one 0.853. After the change of units, the tree keeps exactly 0.903 (Proposition 2.2), while 15-NN falls to 0.813, the SVM to 0.803 and the MLP to 0.777.

After the rotation, 15-NN and the SVM are unchanged and the tree is not (0.920). Standardizing features is a choice of geometry.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Trees ignore changes of units but not rotations; $k$-NN and Gaussian kernels the reverse.
-   The cross-entropy gradient $p - y$ never saturates; the squared loss gradient carries $p(1 - p)$.
-   ReLU networks are piecewise affine; convolutions are the translation-equivariant linear maps.
-   Kernel methods are linear in a feature space: $\alpha = (K + \lambda I)^{-1} y$.
:::

## 3. Graphs and embeddings {#ch3}

High-dimensional data are not spread uniformly: they sit near thin sets with a small intrinsic dimension and sometimes a marked curvature. This chapter measures these properties, then builds graphs that capture them and embeddings that display them.

### 3.1 Normal distributions are… bubbles!

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.1 — Gaussian bubbles]{.tag} Let $X, Y$ be independent $\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ vectors.

(a) For every $\delta > 0$,
$$
\mathbb{P}\Big( \Big| \frac{\|X\|^2}{d} - 1 \Big| \geq \delta \Big) \leq \frac{2}{d\, \delta^2} .
$$

(b) $\mathbb{E} \langle X, Y \rangle = 0$ and $\operatorname{Var} \langle X, Y \rangle = d$, so the cosine of their angle is of order $1/\sqrt d$.

(c) The midpoint $(X + Y)/2$ is $\mathcal{N}(0, I_d / 2)$, with norm close to $\sqrt{d/2}$.

::: proof
(a) is Chebyshev's inequality with Proposition 0.7. (b) $\langle X, Y \rangle = \sum_k X_k Y_k$ is a sum of $d$ independent centred terms of variance 1. (c) A sum of independent Gaussian vectors is Gaussian, with the sum of the covariances. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The density is largest at the origin, yet almost no sample lies near it: the mass sits on a thin shell of radius $\sqrt d$, a bubble. Two samples are almost orthogonal, and their straight-line midpoint is atypical. In the latent space of a generative model, one interpolates along great circles of the shell rather than along chords.

::: ex
[Code 3.2 — Measuring the bubble in dimension 512]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d = 512                                            # e.g. the latent space of a generative model
X, Y = rng.normal(size=(2, 10_000, d))
nx = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1)
print(f"|X|: mean {nx.mean():.2f}, std {nx.std():.3f}   (sqrt(d) = {np.sqrt(d):.2f})")
cos = np.sum(X * Y, axis=1) / (nx * np.linalg.norm(Y, axis=1))
print(f"cosine of two samples: mean {cos.mean():+.4f}, std {cos.std():.4f}   (1/sqrt(d) = {1/np.sqrt(d):.4f})")
mid = np.linalg.norm((X + Y) / 2, axis=1)
print(f"|midpoint|: mean {mid.mean():.2f}, i.e. {(nx.mean() - mid.mean()) / nx.std():.1f} standard deviations inside the shell")
```

The norms are $22.61 \pm 0.70$ for $\sqrt{512} = 22.63$, and the cosines have standard deviation 0.0445, close to $1/\sqrt{512} = 0.0442$. The midpoints have norm 15.98, 9.4 standard deviations inside the shell.
:::

### 3.2 The manifold hypothesis

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — Manifold hypothesis]{.tag} Data in $\mathbb{R}^D$ satisfy the manifold hypothesis if they concentrate near a smooth submanifold $\mathcal{M}$ of dimension $m \ll D$. Near each of its points, $\mathcal{M}$ is the graph of a smooth function of $m$ coordinates.
:::

The images of one object under rotations and lighting changes form such a set, with $m$ equal to the number of degrees of freedom. On $\mathcal{M}$, the relevant distance follows the manifold rather than the chord, and the covering argument of Proposition 1.2 costs $\varepsilon^{-m}$ instead of $\varepsilon^{-D}$. Fefferman, Mitter and Narayanan (2016) give a statistical test of the hypothesis.

### 3.3 Dimension

::: def
[Definition 3.4 — Correlation dimension]{.tag} Let $C(r)$ be the fraction of pairs of samples at distance less than $r$. If $C(r) \propto r^m$ over a range of scales, $m$ is the correlation dimension (Grassberger and Procaccia, 1983).
:::

The range matters: below the noise level, data look $D$-dimensional. Nearest-neighbour estimators avoid choosing it.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — The TwoNN estimator]{.tag} Assume the samples form, near each point, a Poisson process of constant density on an $m$-dimensional manifold. Let $r_1 < r_2$ be the distances from a sample to its two nearest neighbours, and $\mu = r_2 / r_1$. Then
$$
\mathbb{P}(\mu > x) = x^{-m} \quad (x \geq 1),
$$
so $\log \mu$ is exponential with rate $m$, and the maximum likelihood estimator from $N$ samples is
$$
\hat m = \frac{N}{\sum_{i = 1}^N \log \mu_i} .
$$

::: proof
Given $r_2$, the nearest neighbour of a Poisson process is uniform in the $m$-dimensional ball of radius $r_2$, so $\mathbb{P}(r_1 \leq s \mid r_2) = (s / r_2)^m$. Hence $\mathbb{P}(\mu > x) = \mathbb{P}(r_1 < r_2 / x) = x^{-m}$.

The log-likelihood of $N$ independent exponential variables is $N \log m - m \sum_i \log \mu_i$, maximal at $\hat m$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This estimator is due to Facco, d'Errico, Rodriguez and Laio (2017). It is invariant under isometries and under scaling, and it needs no choice of radius.

### 3.4 Curvature

::: def
[Definition 3.6 — Gaussian curvature by circles]{.tag} On a surface, let $C(r)$ be the perimeter of the geodesic circle of radius $r$ around a point. The Gaussian curvature $K$ at that point is defined by
$$
C(r) = 2 \pi r \Big( 1 - \frac{K r^2}{6} + o(r^2) \Big) .
$$
:::

On a sphere of radius $R$, $C(r) = 2 \pi R \sin(r / R)$, hence $K = 1 / R^2$. In the hyperbolic plane of ch. 5, $C(r) = 2 \pi \sinh r$, hence $K = -1$. Positive curvature appears with normalized embeddings and directions; negative curvature appears with hierarchies, whose number of descendants grows exponentially with depth.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.7 — Angle defects add up to topology]{.tag} On a closed polyhedral surface with $V$ vertices, $E$ edges and $F$ faces, let the angle defect at $v$ be $\delta_v = 2\pi - \sum (\text{angles of the faces at } v)$. Then
$$
\sum_v \delta_v = 2 \pi (V - E + F) .
$$

Proof in [ch. 8](#ch8).
::::

For a cube, each of the 8 vertices has defect $\pi/2$, for a total of $4\pi = 2\pi \times 2$. The angle defect is the discrete Gaussian curvature of a mesh.

### 3.5 Neighbourhood graphs and embeddings

::: def
[Definition 3.8 — Neighbourhood graph and Laplacian]{.tag} On samples $x_1, \dots, x_n$, a $k$-NN graph (or $\varepsilon$-graph) carries weights $w_{ij} = \exp(-\|x_i - x_j\|^2 / 2\sigma^2)$ on its edges. With the degree matrix $D = \operatorname{diag}(\sum_j w_{ij})$, the graph Laplacian is $L = D - W$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.9 — Laplacian eigenmaps]{.tag} (a) For every $f \in \mathbb{R}^n$,
$$
f^\top L f = \frac12 \sum_{i, j} w_{ij} (f_i - f_j)^2 \geq 0 .
$$

(b) Among $Y \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ with $Y^\top D Y = I$ and $Y^\top D \mathbf{1} = 0$, the trace $\operatorname{tr}(Y^\top L Y)$ is minimized by the generalized eigenvectors $L v = \lambda D v$ of the $p$ smallest non-zero eigenvalues (Belkin and Niyogi, 2003).

Proof in [ch. 8](#ch8).
::::

Close points get close coordinates, because $(f_i - f_j)^2$ is paid with weight $w_{ij}$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.10 — Classical multidimensional scaling]{.tag} Let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be centred points of $\mathbb{R}^p$, $\Delta_{ij} = \|x_i - x_j\|^2$, and $J = I - \frac1n \mathbf{1} \mathbf{1}^\top$. Then
$$
B = -\tfrac12\, J \Delta J = X X^\top ,
$$
so the eigenvectors of the $p$ largest eigenvalues of $B$, scaled by their square roots, recover the points up to an orthogonal map.

Proof in [ch. 8](#ch8).
::::

Isomap (Tenenbaum, de Silva and Langford, 2000) applies classical scaling to shortest-path distances in a $k$-NN graph, an estimate of geodesic distances on $\mathcal{M}$. When the distances are not Euclidean, $B$ has negative eigenvalues, which measure the distortion.

::: def
[Definition 3.11 — t-SNE and UMAP]{.tag} *t-SNE* (van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008) defines Gaussian affinities $p_{ij}$ in the data, with a width per point set by a target perplexity. It then places points $y_i$ in the plane to minimize $\mathrm{KL}(P \,\|\, Q)$, where
$$
q_{ij} \propto \big( 1 + \|y_i - y_j\|^2 \big)^{-1} .
$$

*UMAP* (McInnes, Healy and Melville, 2018) builds a weighted $k$-NN graph with weights $w_{ij} \in [0, 1]$ and low-dimensional similarities $v_{ij} = (1 + a \|y_i - y_j\|^{2b})^{-1}$. It minimizes the edge-wise binary cross-entropy
$$
\sum_{i \neq j} \Big[ w_{ij} \log \frac{w_{ij}}{v_{ij}} + (1 - w_{ij}) \log \frac{1 - w_{ij}}{1 - v_{ij}} \Big] .
$$
:::

The heavy tails of $q$ and $v$ let clusters separate in the plane. In exchange, the sizes of clusters and the gaps between them carry no metric meaning.

::: ex
[Code 3.12 — Lab: dimension and visualization of the digits]{.tag} TwoNN is checked on a swiss roll and applied to the scikit-learn digits. Four planar embeddings are scored by trustworthiness (are 2D neighbours true neighbours?) and by 10-NN accuracy in the plane. With `umap-learn` installed, add `umap.UMAP()` to the dictionary.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits, make_swiss_roll
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.manifold import Isomap, SpectralEmbedding, TSNE, trustworthiness
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier, NearestNeighbors

def two_nn(Z):
    """TwoNN estimator of the intrinsic dimension (Proposition 3.5)."""
    dist, _ = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=3).fit(Z).kneighbors(Z)
    mu = dist[:, 2] / dist[:, 1]                     # column 0 is the point itself
    return len(Z) / np.sum(np.log(mu))

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
S, _ = make_swiss_roll(n_samples=4000, random_state=0)
Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(30, 30)))       # isometric copy of the roll in R^30
print(f"TwoNN: swiss roll in R^3 {two_nn(S):.2f}, in R^30 {two_nn(np.c_[S, np.zeros((4000, 27))] @ Q.T):.2f}")

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)                  # 1797 images of 8 x 8 pixels, in R^64
X = X / 16.0
print(f"TwoNN: digits in R^64 {two_nn(np.unique(X, axis=0)):.2f}")
methods = {"PCA": PCA(2),
           "Isomap (k=10)": Isomap(n_neighbors=10, n_components=2),
           "Laplacian eigenmaps": SpectralEmbedding(2, n_neighbors=10, random_state=0),
           "t-SNE": TSNE(2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=0)}
for name, m in methods.items():
    Y = m.fit_transform(X)
    tw = trustworthiness(X, Y, n_neighbors=10)       # are 2D neighbours true neighbours?
    acc = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(10), Y, y, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{name:20s} trustworthiness {tw:.3f}   10-NN accuracy in 2D {acc:.3f}")
```

The roll has dimension 1.99 in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and in $\mathbb{R}^{30}$, the digits about 9, far below 64. Trustworthiness and accuracy are 0.830 and 0.613 for PCA, 0.838 and 0.711 for Isomap, 0.929 and 0.915 for Laplacian eigenmaps, 0.993 and 0.974 for t-SNE. Graph-based methods preserve neighbourhoods, not large distances.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   A Gaussian in dimension $d$ is a thin bubble of radius $\sqrt d$; two samples are almost orthogonal.
-   Local methods pay for the intrinsic dimension, which TwoNN estimates by $N / \sum \log(r_2 / r_1)$.
-   Curvature is read on the growth of circles; angle defects are its discrete version.
-   Neighbourhood graphs give embeddings: eigenmaps, Isomap, t-SNE and UMAP.
:::

## 4. Geometric deep learning {#ch4}

Convolutions are the linear layers that respect translations (Proposition 2.10). This chapter builds the layers that respect the symmetries of graphs and of point clouds, then tests them on two scientific problems.

### 4.1 Convolutions on graphs

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Graph signals and permutation equivariance]{.tag} A graph with $n$ nodes has an adjacency matrix $A$ and node features $H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times c}$.

A permutation matrix $P$ relabels the nodes: $A \mapsto P A P^\top$ and $H \mapsto P H$. A layer $\Phi$ is permutation-equivariant if
$$
\Phi(P A P^\top, P H) = P\, \Phi(A, H) .
$$
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — Message passing]{.tag} A message-passing layer updates each node from its neighbourhood $\mathcal{N}(i)$:
$$
h_i' = \phi\Big( h_i,\ \bigoplus_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \psi(h_i, h_j, e_{ij}) \Big),
$$
where $\psi$ and $\phi$ are learned functions, $e_{ij}$ are edge features, and $\bigoplus$ is a symmetric aggregation (sum, mean or maximum).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — Message passing is permutation-equivariant]{.tag} Every layer of Definition 4.2 satisfies Definition 4.1.

::: proof
Relabelling the nodes by $\pi$ sends the neighbourhood of $i$ to that of $\pi(i)$, with the same features. A symmetric aggregation depends only on the multiset of messages, so the new feature of $\pi(i)$ equals the old feature of $i$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — Spectral filters]{.tag} Let $L = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2} = U \Lambda U^\top$ be the normalized Laplacian. The graph Fourier transform of a signal $x$ is $U^\top x$, and a spectral filter is
$$
g(L)\, x = U g(\Lambda) U^\top x .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Polynomial filters are local]{.tag} For a polynomial filter $p(L) = \sum_{k \leq K} \theta_k L^k$, the output at node $i$ depends only on nodes at graph distance at most $K$ from $i$. Moreover, $p(P L P^\top) = P\, p(L)\, P^\top$.

::: proof
$L$ has the sparsity pattern of $A + I$, so $(L^k)_{ij}$ is a sum over walks of length $k$ from $i$ to $j$, and vanishes beyond distance $k$.

The second identity holds for each power, since $P^\top P = I$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The graph convolutional network (GCN) of Kipf and Welling (2017) keeps degree 1 with a renormalization, $H' = \sigma(\hat A H W)$, where
$$
\hat A = \tilde D^{-1/2} (A + I) \tilde D^{-1/2} .
$$
Stacking many such layers averages features over larger and larger regions until all nodes look alike, which is called over-smoothing (Exercise 16).

### 4.2 Point clouds and equivariance

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Euclidean equivariance]{.tag} A map $\Phi$ from point clouds $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 3}$ to point clouds is $E(3)$-equivariant if, for every orthogonal $Q$ and translation $t$,
$$
\Phi(x Q^\top + \mathbf{1} t^\top) = \Phi(x)\, Q^\top + \mathbf{1} t^\top .
$$
A map to features is invariant if its output does not change.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.7 — An equivariant update]{.tag} For any function $\phi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the update
$$
x_i' = x_i + \frac1n \sum_j (x_i - x_j)\, \phi\big( \|x_i - x_j\|^2 \big)
$$
is $E(3)$-equivariant (Satorras, Hoogeboom and Welling, 2021).

::: proof
Distances are invariant. Differences $x_i - x_j$ do not see translations and rotate with $Q$, so the sum rotates with $Q$; adding $x_i$ restores the translation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A point-cloud convolution sums $g(x_j - x_i)\, f_j$ over the neighbours of $x_i$. For rotation invariance, the offset must be expressed in a local frame (normal and tangent directions), and tangent directions are defined only up to rotation.

### 4.3 Five major challenges

The official text announces five challenges without naming them. These notes propose the following five, each discussed elsewhere on the page.

1.  **Choosing the graph.** Neighbourhoods depend on the sampling density and the scale (ch. 3).
2.  **Invariance.** Rigid motions, local frames and orientation ambiguities (Section 4.2).
3.  **Discretization.** A surface can be a mesh, a point cloud or a voxel grid at any resolution; predictions should not depend on that choice (ch. 6).
4.  **Scale.** Shapes have $10^5$ to $10^6$ points, so neighbour searches and memory dominate (ch. 7).
5.  **Data.** Medical data sets often hold tens of labelled shapes, so priors such as invariances must carry the information.

### 4.4 Case study: protein docking

Proteins interact through their surfaces, where shape and chemistry must be complementary. MaSIF (Gainza and coauthors, 2020) computes a mesh of the molecular surface, cuts geodesic patches and applies learned filters in local polar coordinates. dMaSIF (Sverrisson, Feydy, Correia and Bronstein, 2021) samples points directly on a level set of a smooth distance to the atoms. It computes chemical and curvature features there and convolves them in local frames, end to end and much faster.

:::: def
[Definition 4.8 — Smooth distance to a molecule]{.tag} For atom centres $a_1, \dots, a_K$ and a smoothing scale $s > 0$, let
$$
\mathrm{SD}(x) = -s \log \sum_{k = 1}^K \exp\big( -\|x - a_k\| / s \big) .
$$
It is smooth away from the centres, and
$$
\min_k \|x - a_k\| - s \log K \leq \mathrm{SD}(x) \leq \min_k \|x - a_k\| .
$$

::: proof
The sum lies between its largest term, $e^{-\min_k \|x - a_k\| / s}$, and $K$ times that term; take $-s \log$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A surface is the level set $\mathrm{SD} = r$, and points are pushed onto it by Newton-like steps along $\nabla \mathrm{SD}$. The construction is a log-sum-exp (Proposition 0.9), the same reduction as in ch. 6 and 7.

### 4.5 Case study: lung registration

Comparing inhale and exhale CT scans of a patient requires a deformation matching the two vessel trees, extracted as point clouds without correspondences; branches may be missing in either scan. Registration minimizes
$$
\mathcal{D}\big( \varphi_\sharp \mu_{\text{source}}, \mu_{\text{target}} \big) + \mathcal{R}(\varphi)
$$
over deformations $\varphi$. Here $\mathcal{D}$ compares measures without correspondences (a kernel norm or a transport cost, ch. 6), and $\mathcal{R}$ penalizes irregular deformations.

Shen, Feydy and coauthors (2021) combine robust optimal transport, which allows mass to appear or vanish where branches are missing, with learned point features and smooth deformation models.

### 4.6 Should we learn our graphs?

A fixed geometric graph, such as a $k$-NN graph in space, encodes prior knowledge at a cost $O(nk)$. Dynamic graph CNNs (Wang and coauthors, 2019) recompute the $k$-NN graph in feature space at every layer. Transformers go further and learn a dense graph.

::: def
[Definition 4.9 — Self-attention]{.tag} With $Q = H W_Q$, $K = H W_K$ and $V = H W_V$, a self-attention layer computes
$$
H' = \operatorname{softmax}_{\text{rows}}\Big( \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \Big) V .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.10 — Attention is message passing on the complete graph]{.tag} Self-attention is a message-passing layer on the complete graph, with weights $a_{ij}$ given by the softmax and messages $v_j$. It is permutation-equivariant, so without positional encodings it ignores the order of the tokens.

::: proof
Row $i$ of the output is $\sum_j a_{ij} v_j$, an aggregation over all nodes. Relabelling by $P$ gives $Q' = P Q$, $K' = P K$ and $V' = P V$.

The softmax acts row by row, so the attention matrix becomes $P\, \mathcal{A}\, P^\top$, and the output is
$$
P \mathcal{A} P^\top P V = P\, \mathcal{A} V .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A learned dense graph is flexible but costs $O(n^2)$ and needs data or positional encodings to recover geometry. A fixed graph is cheap and encodes geometry, but it cannot adapt to the task. Section 6.5 shows that the attention matrix is a normalized Gaussian kernel.

::: ex
[Code 4.11 — Lab: a graph convolutional network from scratch]{.tag} A two-layer GCN is trained on Zachary's karate club (bundled with NetworkX) with one labelled member per club; then the update of Proposition 4.7 is tested. PyTorch Geometric's `GCNConv` implements the same propagation.

```python
import networkx as nx
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)
torch.set_num_threads(1)
G = nx.karate_club_graph()                                   # 34 members, 78 friendships
y = torch.tensor([G.nodes[i]["club"] == "Officer" for i in G]).long()
A = torch.tensor(nx.to_numpy_array(G, weight=None), dtype=torch.float32) + torch.eye(34)
dinv = A.sum(1).rsqrt()
A_hat = dinv[:, None] * A * dinv[None, :]                    # D^-1/2 (A + I) D^-1/2

class GCN(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_in, n_hid, n_out):
        super().__init__()
        self.W1 = torch.nn.Linear(n_in, n_hid)
        self.W2 = torch.nn.Linear(n_hid, n_out)
    def forward(self, H):                                    # two rounds of message passing
        H = torch.relu(A_hat @ self.W1(H))
        return A_hat @ self.W2(H)

X = torch.eye(34)                                            # no node features: one-hot identities
train = torch.tensor([0, 33])                                # one labelled member per club
model = GCN(34, 16, 2)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01, weight_decay=5e-4)
for step in range(200):
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X)[train], y[train])
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
pred = model(X).argmax(1)
print(f"accuracy on the 32 unlabelled members: {(pred == y).float()[2:].mean():.3f}")

# An E(n)-equivariant layer (Proposition 4.7): messages use only squared distances.
phi = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(1, 16), torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Linear(16, 1))
def egnn_step(x):
    diff = x[:, None, :] - x[None, :, :]                     # x_i - x_j
    w = phi((diff**2).sum(-1, keepdim=True))                 # invariant weights
    return x + (diff * w).mean(1)

x = torch.randn(50, 3)
Q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(torch.randn(3, 3))                    # random orthogonal matrix
t = torch.randn(3)
with torch.no_grad():
    err = (egnn_step(x @ Q.T + t) - (egnn_step(x) @ Q.T + t)).abs().max()
print(f"equivariance error of the layer: {err:.1e}")
```

With two labels, the GCN classifies 31 of the 32 other members correctly (0.969): the graph alone carries the split of the club. The equivariance error, $4.8 \times 10^{-7}$, is float32 rounding.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Message passing with a symmetric aggregation commutes with relabellings; degree-$K$ spectral filters are $K$-hop.
-   Layers built on distances and differences are $E(3)$-equivariant.
-   Protein surfaces and vessel trees are point clouds; registration compares measures.
-   Attention is message passing on a learned complete graph, at cost $O(n^2)$.
:::

## 5. Riemannian metrics and geodesics {#ch5}

When data live on a curved space, straight lines leave the space and averages fall off it. This chapter replaces them by geodesics and Fréchet means, in continuous models and in their discrete approximations.

### 5.1 Metrics, geodesics and means

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Riemannian metric, length, distance]{.tag} A Riemannian metric on a manifold $\mathcal{M}$ is a smoothly varying inner product $g_x$ on each tangent space $T_x \mathcal{M}$. The length of a curve and the distance are
$$
L(\gamma) = \int_0^1 \sqrt{g_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma, \dot\gamma)}\, dt, \qquad d(x, y) = \inf_{\gamma(0) = x,\ \gamma(1) = y} L(\gamma) .
$$
Geodesics are the constant-speed curves that locally minimize length.
:::

::: def
[Definition 5.2 — Exponential and logarithm maps]{.tag} $\exp_x(v)$ is the point reached at time 1 by the geodesic leaving $x$ with velocity $v$, and $\log_x$ is its local inverse. On the unit sphere,
$$
\exp_x(v) = \cos(\|v\|)\, x + \sin(\|v\|)\, \frac{v}{\|v\|}, \qquad d(x, y) = \arccos \langle x, y \rangle .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — Fréchet mean]{.tag} Where the logarithms are defined, the function $F(x) = \frac{1}{2n} \sum_i d(x, x_i)^2$ has Riemannian gradient
$$
\operatorname{grad} F(x) = -\frac1n \sum_i \log_x(x_i) .
$$
A Fréchet mean (a minimizer of $F$) therefore satisfies $\sum_i \log_x(x_i) = 0$, and the iteration
$$
x \leftarrow \exp_x\Big( \frac1n \sum_i \log_x(x_i) \Big)
$$
is gradient descent with unit step.

::: proof
The gradient of $\frac12 d(\cdot, y)^2$ at $x$ is $-\log_x(y)$, a consequence of the Gauss lemma (Lee, 2018); sum over $i$. In $\mathbb{R}^d$, $\log_x(y) = y - x$ and the iteration returns the arithmetic mean in one step. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 5.2 The Poincaré disk

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — Poincaré disk]{.tag} The Poincaré disk is $\mathbb{D} = \{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1 \}$ with the metric $ds = 2 |dz| / (1 - |z|^2)$. Its distance is
$$
d(z, w) = \operatorname{arcosh}\Big( 1 + \frac{2 |z - w|^2}{(1 - |z|^2)(1 - |w|^2)} \Big) .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — Geometry of the disk]{.tag} (a) $d(0, r) = 2 \operatorname{artanh} r = \log \frac{1 + r}{1 - r}$ for $0 \leq r < 1$.

(b) The maps $z \mapsto e^{i\theta} (z - a) / (1 - \bar a z)$, for $|a| < 1$, are isometries. Geodesics are the diameters and the circular arcs orthogonal to the boundary.

(c) The geodesic circle of radius $R$ has perimeter $2 \pi \sinh R$, so the curvature is $K = -1$.

::: proof
(a) The metric depends only on $|z|$, and along any curve $|\dot\gamma| \geq \big| \tfrac{d}{dt} |\gamma| \big|$. A curve from 0 to $r$ therefore has length at least
$$
\int_0^r \frac{2\, dt}{1 - t^2} = 2 \operatorname{artanh} r ,
$$
with equality along the radius.

(b) For these maps, $|\varphi'(z)| / (1 - |\varphi(z)|^2) = 1 / (1 - |z|^2)$, so they preserve $ds$. They send diameters to circles orthogonal to the boundary, and they move any point to 0, where (a) gives the distance formula.

(c) The circle is the Euclidean circle of radius $\rho = \tanh(R/2)$, of hyperbolic perimeter $2 \pi \rho \cdot 2 / (1 - \rho^2) = 2 \pi \sinh R$. Compare with Definition 3.6: $2\pi \sinh R = 2 \pi R (1 + R^2/6 + \dots)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The boundary is infinitely far: $d(0, 0.9) = 2.944$ and $d(0, 0.99) = 5.293$. Perimeters grow like $e^R$, like the number of nodes of a tree at depth $R$. Trees therefore embed in the disk with arbitrarily small distortion (Sarkar, 2011), but not in a Euclidean plane, which motivates hyperbolic embeddings of hierarchies (Nickel and Kiela, 2017).

::: ex
[Code 5.6 — Lab: distances, isometries and circles in the disk]{.tag} The official lab uses GeomStats; the formulas are short enough to write in NumPy.

```python
import numpy as np

def dist(z, w):
    """Geodesic distance in the Poincare disk (Definition 5.4)."""
    return np.arccosh(1 + 2 * abs(z - w)**2 / ((1 - abs(z)**2) * (1 - abs(w)**2)))

def mobius(z, a, theta=0.0):
    """Isometry of the disk sending a to 0."""
    return np.exp(1j * theta) * (z - a) / (1 - np.conj(a) * z)

for r in [0.5, 0.9, 0.99]:
    print(f"d(0, {r}) = {dist(0, r):.4f}   log((1+r)/(1-r)) = {np.log((1 + r) / (1 - r)):.4f}")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
z, w = 0.5 * (rng.random(2) + 1j * rng.random(2))
a = 0.3 - 0.6j
print(f"isometry check: {dist(z, w):.6f} = {dist(mobius(z, a, 1.0), mobius(w, a, 1.0)):.6f}")

for R in [1.0, 3.0, 6.0]:                     # perimeter of the geodesic circle of radius R
    rho = np.tanh(R / 2)                      # Euclidean radius of that circle
    pts = rho * np.exp(2j * np.pi * np.arange(100_000) / 100_000)
    perim = np.sum(dist(pts, np.roll(pts, 1)))
    print(f"R = {R}: perimeter {perim:10.2f}   2 pi sinh R = {2 * np.pi * np.sinh(R):10.2f}"
          f"   2 pi R = {2 * np.pi * R:6.2f}")
```

The distance formula matches (a) at $r = 0.5$, 0.9 and 0.99 (1.0986, 2.9444, 5.2933), and the Möbius map preserves a random distance. The perimeters of circles of radius 1, 3 and 6 are 7.38, 62.94 and 1267.4, against 6.28, 18.85 and 37.70 in the plane.
:::

### 5.3 Discrete and continuous models

A continuous model gives a metric tensor and geodesic equations. A discrete model gives a graph whose edges carry lengths: a $k$-NN graph of samples, the edges of a mesh, or a pixel grid.

::: thm
[Algorithm 5.7 — Dijkstra, 1959]{.tag} From a source $s$, with non-negative edge lengths $\ell_{uv}$: set $\delta(s) = 0$ and $\delta = \infty$ elsewhere. Repeatedly settle the unsettled node $u$ with the smallest $\delta(u)$, and for each neighbour $v$ of $u$ set
$$
\delta(v) \leftarrow \min\big( \delta(v), \delta(u) + \ell_{uv} \big) .
$$

*Correctness*: when $u$ is settled, any other path to $u$ leaves the settled set through a node whose tentative value is already at least $\delta(u)$, and lengths are non-negative. With a binary heap, the cost is $O((n + m) \log n)$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.8 — Graph distances approximate geodesics]{.tag} Let samples cover a compact submanifold densely compared with its curvature radius, and connect points closer than $\varepsilon$. For suitable $\varepsilon$, the graph distances $d_G$ satisfy, with small $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$,
$$
(1 - \lambda_1)\, d_{\mathcal{M}} \leq d_G \leq (1 + \lambda_2)\, d_{\mathcal{M}} .
$$

::: proof
See Bernstein, de Silva, Langford and Tenenbaum (2000), and the sketch in [ch. 8](#ch8). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The theorem needs samples spread in all directions. On a regular grid, it fails.

::: ex
[Example 5.9 — Metrication error of grids]{.tag} On a 4-neighbour pixel grid, the graph distance is the $\ell^1$ norm: from $(0, 0)$ to $(40, 40)$ it is 80 instead of 56.57, an error of 41 %. On an 8-neighbour grid the diagonal is exact, but to $(40, 20)$ the graph distance is
$$
20 \sqrt 2 + 20 = 48.28 \quad \text{instead of} \quad \sqrt{2000} = 44.72 ,
$$
an error of 8 % that no grid refinement removes.
:::

### 5.4 Shortest paths

The distance $u(x) = d(x_0, x)$ solves the eikonal equation $\|\nabla u\| = 1/F$ in a medium of speed $F$. Fast marching (Sethian, 1996) solves it in Dijkstra's order with a consistent local update, so the error vanishes with the grid step. The heat method (Crane, Weischedel and Wardetzky, 2013) diffuses heat briefly, normalizes its gradient and integrates it, justified by Varadhan's formula.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.10 — Varadhan's formula in $\mathbb{R}^d$]{.tag} The heat kernel $k_t(x, y) = (4 \pi t)^{-d/2} \exp\big( -\|x - y\|^2 / 4t \big)$ satisfies
$$
\lim_{t \to 0}\ -4t \log k_t(x, y) = \|x - y\|^2 .
$$

::: proof
$-4t \log k_t(x, y) = \|x - y\|^2 + 2 d\, t \log(4 \pi t)$, and $t \log t \to 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

On a Riemannian manifold the same limit gives $d_{\mathcal{M}}(x, y)^2$ (Varadhan, 1967). A Gaussian kernel at small scale is a geodesic distance in disguise: kernels and manifolds meet here.

### 5.5 Practical applications

Hierarchies are embedded in the Poincaré disk. Directions, rotations and diffusion tensors are averaged by Fréchet means on spheres, rotation groups and positive matrices. Geodesic distances on anatomical surfaces give pose-independent descriptors. GeomStats (Miolane and coauthors, 2020) implements these spaces.

::: ex
[Code 5.11 — Lab: a Fréchet mean on the sphere and grid shortest paths]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import lil_matrix
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import dijkstra

def exp_map(x, v):                            # unit sphere: follow the great circle
    t = np.linalg.norm(v)
    return x if t < 1e-12 else np.cos(t) * x + np.sin(t) * v / t

def log_map(x, y):                            # inverse of exp_map at x
    c = np.clip(x @ y, -1, 1)
    u = y - c * x
    n = np.linalg.norm(u)
    return np.zeros(3) if n < 1e-12 else np.arccos(c) * u / n

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
north = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])
pts = [exp_map(north, np.r_[0.6 * rng.normal(size=2), 0]) for _ in range(50)]
x = pts[0]
for it in range(20):                          # Riemannian gradient descent (Proposition 5.3)
    g = np.mean([log_map(x, p) for p in pts], axis=0)
    x = exp_map(x, g)
print(f"Frechet mean {np.round(x, 4)}, gradient norm {np.linalg.norm(g):.1e}")
e = np.mean(pts, axis=0)
print(f"Euclidean mean {np.round(e, 4)}, norm {np.linalg.norm(e):.4f} (off the sphere)")

n = 41                                        # grid graphs: discrete shortest paths
idx = lambda i, j: i * n + j
for name, steps in [("4-neighbour", [(0, 1), (1, 0)]),
                    ("8-neighbour", [(0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1), (1, -1)])]:
    W = lil_matrix((n * n, n * n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            for di, dj in steps:
                if 0 <= i + di < n and 0 <= j + dj < n:
                    W[idx(i, j), idx(i + di, j + dj)] = np.hypot(di, dj)
    D = dijkstra(W.tocsr(), directed=False, indices=idx(0, 0))
    for (i, j) in [(40, 0), (40, 40), (40, 20)]:
        print(f"{name}: to ({i:2d},{j:2d}) graph {D[idx(i, j)]:6.2f}, Euclidean {np.hypot(i, j):6.2f}")
```

After 20 iterations the gradient norm is $2 \times 10^{-13}$. The Euclidean mean of the same points has norm 0.70: it lies inside the ball, off the sphere. The grid distances reproduce Example 5.9: 80.00 and 60.00 on the 4-neighbour grid, 56.57 and 48.28 on the 8-neighbour grid.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Fréchet means solve $\sum_i \log_x(x_i) = 0$, by Riemannian gradient descent.
-   The Poincaré disk has curvature $-1$, circles of perimeter $2\pi \sinh R$, and room for trees.
-   Graph distances approximate geodesics on spread samples; grids keep a metrication error.
-   Varadhan's formula turns a small-time heat kernel into a squared geodesic distance.
:::

## 6. Probability distributions {#ch6}

Histograms, densities, point clouds and populations are probability distributions. This chapter compares them pointwise, by blurring and by moving mass, then shows that one matrix underlies kernels, graphs, transport and attention.

### 6.1 Geometry in statistics

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Measures and three families of discrepancies]{.tag} A point cloud $x_1, \dots, x_n$ with weights $a_i \geq 0$ summing to 1 is the measure $\alpha = \sum_i a_i \delta_{x_i}$. Discrepancies between measures fall into three families:

-   *divergences*, which compare densities at the same location: total variation, Hellinger, Kullback–Leibler;
-   *kernel norms*, which blur the measures with a kernel, then compare them;
-   *transport costs*, which measure the effort to move one measure onto the other.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Divergences ignore the ground distance]{.tag} If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have disjoint supports, then $\mathrm{TV}(\alpha, \beta) = 1$ and $\mathrm{KL}(\alpha \,\|\, \beta) = +\infty$, however close the supports are.

::: proof
Total variation is $\sup_A |\alpha(A) - \beta(A)|$; take $A$ the support of $\alpha$. KL is infinite as soon as $\alpha$ charges a set where $\beta$ vanishes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For $\delta_0$ and $\delta_t$, the values are the same for $t = 0.01$ and $t = 100$, so a loss built on them gives no gradient. Point clouds, almost surely disjoint, need the other two families.

### 6.2 Information geometry

::: def
[Definition 6.3 — Fisher information metric]{.tag} For a smooth family of densities $p_\theta$, $\theta \in \Theta \subset \mathbb{R}^k$, the Fisher metric is
$$
g_{ij}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}\big[ \partial_i \log p_\theta(X)\ \partial_j \log p_\theta(X) \big] .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — KL is locally the Fisher metric]{.tag} For a small displacement $\delta$,
$$
\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \,\|\, p_{\theta + \delta}) = \tfrac12\, \delta^\top g(\theta)\, \delta + o(\|\delta\|^2) .
$$

::: proof
Expand $\log p_{\theta + \delta}$ to second order in $\delta$ and take the expectation under $p_\theta$. The first-order term vanishes, since
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \partial_i \log p_\theta = \partial_i \int p_\theta = 0 .
$$
The second-order term is $-\frac12 \delta^\top H \delta$, with $H = \mathbb{E}[\nabla^2 \log p_\theta]$, and $-H = g$ by the same differentiation under the integral. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.5 — Gaussians form a hyperbolic plane]{.tag} For $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, the Fisher metric is $ds^2 = (d\mu^2 + 2\, d\sigma^2) / \sigma^2$. With $x = \mu / \sqrt 2$, this is twice the metric of the hyperbolic half-plane, so
$$
d_{\mathrm{FR}} = \sqrt 2\, \operatorname{arcosh}\Big( 1 + \frac{(\mu_1 - \mu_2)^2 / 2 + (\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2}{2 \sigma_1 \sigma_2} \Big) .
$$

Proof in [ch. 8](#ch8).
::::

Two Gaussians with the same mean and widths $\sigma$ and $2\sigma$ are at distance $\sqrt 2 \log 2 = 0.98$, whatever $\sigma$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.6 — The natural gradient is intrinsic]{.tag} Let $\theta = \phi(\eta)$ be a reparametrization with Jacobian $J$. The natural gradient $g(\theta)^{-1} \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}$ (Amari, 1998) transforms like a velocity, $\Delta \eta = J^{-1} \Delta \theta$, so the update does not depend on the parametrization to first order.

Proof in [ch. 8](#ch8).
::::

### 6.3 Kernel norms

::: def
[Definition 6.7 — Kernel norm, maximum mean discrepancy]{.tag} For a positive definite kernel $k$, the squared kernel norm between measures is
$$
\|\alpha - \beta\|_k^2 = \iint k(x, y)\, d(\alpha - \beta)(x)\, d(\alpha - \beta)(y) .
$$
For point clouds, it is $a^\top K_{xx} a + b^\top K_{yy} b - 2\, a^\top K_{xy} b$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.8 — Dual formula]{.tag} With $m_\alpha = \int k(\cdot, x)\, d\alpha(x)$ the mean embedding in $\mathcal{H}_k$,
$$
\|\alpha - \beta\|_k = \|m_\alpha - m_\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}} = \sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}} \leq 1} \int f\, d(\alpha - \beta) .
$$

::: proof
By the reproducing property, $\int f\, d\alpha = \langle f, m_\alpha \rangle$ in $\mathcal{H}$. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the supremum by $\|m_\alpha - m_\beta\|$, with equality for $f$ proportional to $m_\alpha - m_\beta$. Expanding $\|m_\alpha - m_\beta\|^2$ gives Definition 6.7. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a characteristic kernel, such as the Gaussian, the norm vanishes only if $\alpha = \beta$ (Gretton and coauthors, 2012). The energy distance uses the conditionally positive kernel $k(x, y) = -\|x - y\|$. Kernel norms are cheap and smooth, but a Gaussian kernel of width $\sigma$ hardly sees displacements much larger than $\sigma$.

### 6.4 Optimal transport

::: def
[Definition 6.9 — Optimal transport]{.tag} For a cost $c(x, y)$, the transport cost between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is
$$
\mathrm{OT}(\alpha, \beta) = \min_{\pi \in \Pi(\alpha, \beta)} \int c\, d\pi ,
$$
where $\Pi(\alpha, \beta)$ is the set of couplings, the measures on pairs with marginals $\alpha$ and $\beta$. For $c = \|x - y\|^p$, $W_p = \mathrm{OT}^{1/p}$ is the Wasserstein distance.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.10 — Transport on the line sorts]{.tag} For $n$ points on $\mathbb{R}$ with weights $1/n$ each and a convex cost $c(x, y) = h(x - y)$, sorting both clouds gives an optimal matching. In particular,
$$
W_2^2 = \frac1n \sum_i \big( x_{(i)} - y_{(i)} \big)^2 .
$$

::: proof
For permutation matchings: if $x_1 < x_2$ and $y_1 < y_2$ are crossed, uncrossing does not increase the cost, because
$$
(x_1 - y_2)^2 + (x_2 - y_1)^2 - (x_1 - y_1)^2 - (x_2 - y_2)^2 = 2 (x_2 - x_1)(y_2 - y_1) \geq 0 .
$$
The same argument holds for convex $h$. Couplings with equal weights reduce to permutations by Birkhoff's theorem. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 6.11 — Entropic transport and Sinkhorn divergence]{.tag} For $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$
\mathrm{OT}_\varepsilon(\alpha, \beta) = \min_{\pi \in \Pi(\alpha, \beta)} \int c\, d\pi + \varepsilon\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \alpha \otimes \beta) ,
$$
and the Sinkhorn divergence is
$$
S_\varepsilon(\alpha, \beta) = \mathrm{OT}_\varepsilon(\alpha, \beta) - \tfrac12 \mathrm{OT}_\varepsilon(\alpha, \alpha) - \tfrac12 \mathrm{OT}_\varepsilon(\beta, \beta) .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.12 — The entropic plan scales a Gibbs kernel]{.tag} For discrete measures with weights $a, b$, the optimal entropic plan has the form
$$
\pi_{ij} = a_i b_j \exp\big( (f_i + g_j - c(x_i, y_j)) / \varepsilon \big)
$$
for dual potentials $f, g$, and
$$
\mathrm{OT}_\varepsilon = \langle a, f \rangle + \langle b, g \rangle .
$$

::: proof
The objective is strictly convex in $\pi$. With multipliers $f_i$ and $g_j$ for the marginal constraints, the stationarity condition in $\pi_{ij}$ reads
$$
c_{ij} + \varepsilon \log \frac{\pi_{ij}}{a_i b_j} = f_i + g_j ,
$$
which is the stated form. At the optimum, the entropic term cancels the cost term up to $\langle a, f \rangle + \langle b, g \rangle$, by strong duality (Peyré and Cuturi, 2019). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Algorithm 6.13 — Sinkhorn, in the log domain]{.tag} Alternate the two marginal constraints, starting from $g = 0$:
$$
f_i \leftarrow -\varepsilon \log \sum_j b_j\, e^{(g_j - c_{ij})/\varepsilon}, \qquad g_j \leftarrow -\varepsilon \log \sum_i a_i\, e^{(f_i - c_{ij})/\varepsilon} .
$$
